questions.stem: Why do arteries have thick muscular walls with elastic fibres?

options.explanation: The walls manage pressure, not storage.

options.text: To withstand the high pressure and recoil to maintain it as blood passes
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To absorb oxygen from the blood
options.explanation: Gas exchange never happens in vessel walls.
Arterial flow is fast, not slowed.

questions.stem: Which vessel is the exception that carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart?

options.explanation: That vein returns deoxygenated blood toward the heart.
It carries oxygenated blood toward the heart.
Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
The aorta carries oxygenated blood to the body.

questions.stem: What do valves inside veins achieve?

options.explanation: Veins cannot pump; the heart and muscles move venous blood.
Valves direct flow; they do not pressurise.
Filtering is a kidney and liver job.

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

questions.stem: Why does a vein's large lumen suit its job?

options.text: It reduces resistance to flow under low pressure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: It raises the pressure to heart levels

Lumen width is the bore, not the wall.

options.text: It traps oxygen for the tissues

questions.stem: State three structural differences between arteries and veins.
questions.modelAnswer: Arteries have thick muscular walls, narrow lumens and no valves; veins have thin walls, large lumens and valves.

questions.stem: Name the two exceptions to the usual oxygen content of arteries and veins.
questions.modelAnswer: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood.

questions.stem: Explain why elastic recoil in artery walls matters for steady blood delivery.
questions.modelAnswer: The walls stretch during each pulse and then recoil, smoothing the surge and keeping the pressure up between heartbeats, so flow continues steadily.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a patient's leg veins swollen with pooled blood. Link the finding to a valve problem.
questions.modelAnswer: Faulty valves let venous blood run backwards, so it pools in the low-pressure leg veins instead of riding toward the heart.

questions.stem: How thick is a capillary wall?

options.text: It has no wall at all
options.explanation: A wall exists, just extremely thin.
Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Several cells thick like a vein
options.explanation: Vein walls are layered; capillary walls are not.
Capillaries are the thinnest of the three.

questions.stem: What does the leakiness of capillary walls achieve?

options.explanation: Cells stay inside; only plasma leaks.
Capillaries have no valves.

options.text: Plasma escapes to form tissue fluid around the cells
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Pressure is low in capillaries.

questions.stem: Why does the one-cell-thick wall suit exchange?

options.explanation: Capillaries run at low pressure.
Temperature is irrelevant to the wall's role.
Leakage is precisely the design.

options.text: It gives a very short diffusion distance for substances
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: Both oxygenated and deoxygenated blood, as exchange proceeds along their length
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: At what speed does blood move through capillaries?

options.explanation: The aorta flow far outpaces capillary flow.

options.text: Slowly, giving exchange time to happen
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Arteries are the fast lanes; capillaries crawl.
Blood flows, just slowly.

questions.stem: State the role of capillaries in the circulatory system.
questions.modelAnswer: They exchange substances with the tissues across thin, leaky walls at low pressure.

questions.stem: Name the fluid that leaks from capillaries to surround cells.
questions.modelAnswer: Tissue fluid forms when plasma leaks out of capillaries.

questions.stem: Explain why the slow capillary flow rate is an advantage.
questions.modelAnswer: Slower passage gives more time for diffusion, so oxygen and nutrients leave and wastes enter across the thin wall before the blood moves on.

questions.stem: An athlete's muscles need more glucose during a race. Describe how the capillaries serve that demand.
questions.modelAnswer: Capillaries widen their network in active muscle, and their thin leaky walls deliver glucose and oxygen into the tissue fluid quickly while carrying carbon dioxide away.
